analysis.one_liner: Makes private insurers pay children's Medicaid claims first and requires insurance checks for Medicaid applicants.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in a House subcommittee with zero cosponsors until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change who pays first when a Medicaid patient also has private insurance. It would end the rule that lets Medicaid pay first for children's preventive care and for families in child-support cases, and it would cut off federal Medicaid money for people whose insurance status the state did not check and verify. It would also let states hand their cost-recovery work to the private insurers and managed-care companies that run Medicaid.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, federal and state taxpayers would have benefited modestly, because more Medicaid bills would be pushed to private insurers and managed-care plans to pay first [S2]. States and their contracted health insurers would also have gained new, explicit authority to pursue reimbursement from third parties, with insurers acting as the state's collection agent [S3]. Health insurers and managed-care organizations, including pharmacy benefit managers, would have gained a formalized, contract-based role in Medicaid cost recovery even as they absorbed new first-in-line payment obligations [S3].

how_it_helps.text: It would repeal the two exceptions that let Medicaid pay first and seek reimbursement later — for children's preventive care and for people in child-support cases — so legally liable insurers would have to pay those claims before Medicaid, shifting those costs off state and federal budgets [S2].

It would let states delegate or transfer their right to recover costs from liable third parties to the health insurers and managed-care organizations running Medicaid, and would require states to assure the federal government that those insurers hold the state's legal authority to collect [S3].
It would give insurers 60 days to respond to state inquiries and would treat state-plan authorizations as valid on behalf of Medicaid patients, streamlining the recovery process [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private health insurers and the employers funding group coverage would bear the main cost, since they would have to pay claims for children's preventive care and child-support cases before Medicaid instead of reimbursing later [S2]. State Medicaid agencies would face a new duty to collect and verify third-party insurance information for every applicant, and would forfeit federal matching funds for care provided to anyone whose coverage was not verified — an administrative burden paid for with state dollars and a risk of lost federal funding [S3]. Medicaid beneficiaries, especially children, could face billing delays or enrollment friction if verification stalls [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Private insurers and state Medicaid agencies

drawbacks.text: The verification requirement is a benefit restriction: after January 1, 2023, federal Medicaid payments would be unavailable for any individual whose third-party insurance information the state had not obtained and verified, which in practice creates a paperwork barrier that could delay or block coverage for eligible people who lack documents [S3].

Repealing the Medicaid-first exception for children's preventive pediatric care would shift billing onto private plans and families' other coverage, creating a real risk that routine children's care gets delayed or tangled in payer disputes [S2].

The bill would transfer to health insurers, including managed-care organizations and pharmacy benefit managers, the state's assignment of patients' own rights to payment from third parties, giving private companies collection authority that today rests with government and raising the prospect of recoveries pursued against patients' settlements [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings case is real but modest: making insurers pay first for a defined set of claims shifts costs off Medicaid, and stronger recovery tools claw back money when someone else was responsible. The cost is a new administrative gate on Medicaid enrollment itself — a state that fails to verify insurance status loses federal money for that person's care — plus the risk that children's preventive care becomes a billing fight between payers. On balance, the design trades a modest, hard-to-verify savings for a meaningful risk of coverage delays for low-income families, and no hearing or analysis ever tested that trade.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its Health Subcommittee, and no one ever gave it a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Burgess introduced the bill on February 7, 2022, with no cosponsors [S1].
The same day it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and on February 8 it was referred to that committee's Health Subcommittee, where the action record ends [S5].
No markup, hearing, floor vote, or further action of any kind followed before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill died in subcommittee [S5, S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo won. Health insurers and Medicaid managed-care plans never faced the new requirement to pay children's claims first, and Medicaid beneficiaries were never subjected to the insurance-verification requirement that could have delayed their coverage. Taxpayers also gained nothing, since the projected cost-shift never happened.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers, and beneficiaries spared new verification hurdles

for.name: Rep. Michael Burgess
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and proposed it to the House; it drew no cosponsors from either party

against.name: Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee referred the bill to its Health Subcommittee on February 8, 2022, and never scheduled a markup or hearing; the bill died there

against.name: House members of both parties
against.what_they_did: Not one member of either party signed on as a cosponsor during the bill's year in play

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so no roll-call split exists; the only signals are a lone Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and a Democratically led committee that never took the bill up.

industries.industry: Health insurers and Medicaid managed-care organizations (including pharmacy benefit managers)
industries.note: The bill would have made these companies pay claims for children's preventive care and child-support cases before Medicaid, a direct cost, while simultaneously handing them formal contractual authority to act as the state's recovery agent and to take assignment of patients' third-party payment rights. Their interest runs with taxpayers on the payment mandate but against beneficiaries on the collection powers.

States would have gained a way to shift costs to liable third parties and to delegate collections to contractors, but they would also have borne new verification duties and risked forfeiting federal matching funds for any individual whose insurance status was not checked. As a government interest, its gains mostly align with taxpayers.
